connections.label: Ignorance, surface reading and historical claims

chunks.title: Opening historical question — Did belief in the Mahdi begin only with the third-century birth?
chunks.text:
Mutahhari's historical argument begins by rejecting the idea that belief in Mahdism originated only around the birth of Imam al-Mahdi in the middle of the third century AH.

Mutahhari begins by challenging the claim that Mahdism was invented around the time Imam al-Mahdi was born. His method is historical: trace Qur’anic themes, Prophetic reports, statements attributed to Imam ‘Ali, and earlier movements that used the idea. The existence of a belief and the truth of every claim made in its name are separate questions.

chunks.title: Mahdism in the Qur’an and in the sayings of prophets — General promises of the righteous inheriting the earth
chunks.text:
Mutahhari points to Qur'anic promises concerning the inheritance of the earth by righteous servants and the eventual triumph of true religion as general foundations for belief in a future righteous order.

Mutahhari cites Qur’anic promises that righteous servants will inherit the earth and that the true religion will ultimately prevail. He treats these as broad foundations for the expectation of a just future, not as a complete identification of every detail about the Imam. The distinction is between a general scriptural promise and the further interpretive steps used to connect it to a particular doctrine.

chunks.title: Mahdism in the Qur’an and in the sayings of prophets — Why cross-tradition reports matter
chunks.text:
Mutahhari emphasizes that reports concerning the Promised al-Mahdi are not confined to Shi'ah collections; he cites the existence of substantial Sunni-source material as part of his historical argument.

Mutahhari argues that reports about the Promised Mahdi are found in Sunni as well as Shi‘ah sources. This is relevant to his historical claim that the idea was not a late invention confined to one community. It does not mean every narration has the same authenticity or wording; the existence, provenance, and strength of individual reports still require careful evaluation.

chunks.title: Opening historical question — The doctrine’s effect on Islamic history
chunks.text:
Rather than simply cataloguing Qur'anic verses and hadith, Mutahhari says his principal concern is how belief in the Promised al-Mahdi affected Islamic history.

Mutahhari says his main concern is not to list every verse and narration, but to examine how belief in the Promised Mahdi influenced historical events. This shifts the chapter from doctrinal foundations to political and social history: people invoked the belief to explain uprisings, identify claimants, and interpret the future. Those uses are evidence of historical influence, not proof that every claimant was genuine.

chunks.title: ‘Ali’s saying — The earth is never empty of God’s proof
chunks.text:
Mutahhari quotes the report of Imam 'Ali's conversation with Kumayl, emphasizing the principle that the earth is never empty of God's proof, whether that proof is manifest or hidden.

In the report of Imam ‘Ali’s conversation with Kumayl, the earth is never left without God’s proof, whether that proof is publicly evident or hidden from sight. Mutahhari uses the report to connect the idea of a hidden Imam to an earlier tradition, rather than treating concealment as a concept created only after the birth of Imam al-Mahdi. The report’s transmission and interpretation remain part of the evidence readers should assess.

chunks.title: Mukhtar’s uprising and belief in Mahdism — A political movement uses a religious claim
chunks.text:
Mutahhari identifies Mukhtar's movement as an early historical example in which the Mahdi concept was used politically. Mukhtar presented Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah as the Promised Mahdi and himself as his representative.

Mutahhari describes Mukhtar’s movement to avenge Imam al-Husayn as an early historical case in which the Mahdi concept was used to attract support. Mukhtar presented Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah as the Promised Mahdi and himself as the Imam’s representative. Mutahhari deliberately avoids reducing the whole movement to a simple verdict of good or evil; his focus is how the claim functioned politically.

chunks.title: Mukhtar’s uprising and belief in Mahdism — What happened after Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah’s death?
chunks.text:
After Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah's death, followers associated with this movement maintained that he had not died and was hidden at Mount Radwa. Mutahhari presents this as part of the historical development of Mahdist ideas.

After Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah died, some followers claimed he had not died but was concealed at Mount Radwa until he could fill the earth with justice. Mutahhari links this development to the later Kaysanite movement. The example shows how an existing expectation can be attached to a particular person and then reinterpreted when that person dies; it does not establish the claimant’s identity as true.

chunks.title: The words of Zuhri — Expectation of a future rising from the Ahl al-Bayt
chunks.text:
Mutahhari cites Zuhri's reaction to Zayd ibn 'Ali's uprising as evidence that expectation of a future successful rising from the Prophet's family was already a recognizable idea in early Islamic discourse.

Mutahhari cites a report in which Zuhri, on hearing of Zayd ibn ‘Ali’s uprising, remarks that the time for the Mahdi’s emergence from the Prophet’s family would come. The author uses the reaction to argue that expectation of a future successful rising was already known. He explicitly separates that historical point from whether Zuhri’s criticism of Zayd’s uprising was correct.

chunks.title: The rising of Nafs Zakiyyah and the belief in Mahdism — Why Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allah drew the claim
chunks.text:
The chapter discusses Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah, known as Nafs al-Zakiyyah, and the way people connected claims about him with Mahdism because of lineage, name and other reported signs.

Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allah, known as Nafs Zakiyyah, was associated with the Mahdi claim because of his lineage and reported physical signs. Mutahhari explains that the movement attracted pledges from people who expected a promised leader. The episode illustrates the power of a religious expectation in politics, but the number of pledges does not establish that the identification was correct.

chunks.title: The rising of Nafs Zakiyyah and the belief in Mahdism — Imam al-Sadiq separates justice from false identification
chunks.text:
When invited to support Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah's uprising, Imam al-Sadiq distinguished between supporting an uprising for enjoining good and forbidding evil and accepting the claim that Muhammad was the Promised Mahdi. He rejected the latter identification.

When invited to support Muhammad’s uprising, Imam al-Sadiq reportedly distinguished between a movement for enjoining good and forbidding evil and a movement claiming that Muhammad was the Promised Mahdi. He was willing to support the former purpose but rejected the false identification. The distinction is central: a cause can oppose oppression without every religious claim used to justify its leader being true.

chunks.title: The rising of Nafs Zakiyyah and the belief in Mahdism — Why claims repeatedly attached to Alawi leaders
chunks.text:
Mutahhari argues that the recurrence of Mahdist claims around various Alawi figures itself indicates how deeply established expectation of a future Mahdi was in the Muslim community.

Mutahhari argues that repeated attempts to identify particular Alawi figures as the Mahdi show how widely the expectation was known. The historical inference is about the belief’s presence in the community; it is not that every claimant was authentic. The chapter repeatedly asks readers to distinguish evidence that a belief existed from evidence that a specific individual fulfilled it.

chunks.title: The deceit of Mansur, the Abbasid caliph — A caliph named al-Mahdi
chunks.text:
The chapter notes that an Abbasid caliph was also named al-Mahdi, illustrating how the Mahdi concept had political and historical resonance beyond one specific doctrinal community.

Mutahhari notes that Mansur named his son al-Mahdi and cites reports that the name could be used to suggest that the awaited figure was the Abbasid prince. The example shows that a religiously powerful title can be appropriated for dynastic messaging. The title itself does not prove the person’s identity, and the chapter reports the political interpretation through historical sources rather than direct access to every private motive.

chunks.title: The deceit of Mansur, the Abbasid caliph — Distinguishing a widespread belief from proof of a claimant
chunks.text:
A recurring exam point is that the existence of historical claims about a person being Mahdi does not itself prove the claim. Mutahhari distinguishes what people claimed from what he presents as the underlying doctrinal/historical evidence.

The chapter describes how people sometimes pledged allegiance to a claimant because they believed he was the promised Mahdi, without carefully investigating the claim. Mutahhari treats this as a recurring historical mistake: widespread expectation made the title politically potent, but also made communities vulnerable to appropriation. A belief’s influence and a claimant’s authenticity require different kinds of evidence.

chunks.title: The deceit of Mansur, the Abbasid caliph — Political appropriation of the Mahdi name
chunks.text:
Mutahhari reports that Mansur named his son Mahdi and, according to the historical accounts he cites, sometimes used the name politically while privately acknowledging that neither his son nor 'Abd Allah al-Mahdi was the promised figure.

Mutahhari reports that Mansur could tell different audiences contradictory things about whether his son or ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd was the Promised Mahdi. He uses the contrast to illustrate how rulers may manipulate religious expectations to secure political advantage. Because this is a historical report cited by the author, it should be attributed as such rather than repeated as independently verified access to Mansur’s private thinking.

chunks.title: Muhammad ibn ‘Ijlan and Mansur ‘Abbasi — A mistaken pledge and a severe punishment
chunks.text:
The case of the Medinan scholar Muhammad ibn 'Ijlan illustrates the danger of confusing a claimant with the promised Mahdi. He pledged allegiance to 'Abd Allah al-Mahdi because he believed him to be the promised figure; scholars intervened on his behalf.

The Medinan scholar Muhammad ibn ‘Ijlan pledged allegiance to ‘Abd Allah al-Mahd, apparently believing he was the Promised Mahdi. Mansur ordered punishment, but other scholars interceded and explained that the pledge arose from a mistaken religious identification rather than hostility toward the Abbasids. Mutahhari uses the episode to show how a doctrinal expectation shaped real political choices and exposed people to danger.

chunks.title: Muhammad ibn ‘Ijlan and Mansur ‘Abbasi — What early disputes were actually about
chunks.text:
Mutahhari argues that early disagreements generally concerned which individual was the Mahdi, rather than whether the promised Mahdi existed at all. He cites disputes concerning Imam al-Kazim, Imam al-Baqir, Imam al-Sadiq and others.

Mutahhari argues that many early disputes concerned which individual was the Mahdi, not whether a promised Mahdi existed at all. He cites different claims attached to descendants of the Prophet’s family. This is his summary of the historical evidence; readers should distinguish the broad pattern he identifies from the details and reliability of each report.

chunks.title: Muhammad ibn ‘Ijlan and Mansur ‘Abbasi — Imam al-Sadiq makes Isma‘il’s death public
chunks.text:
The chapter recounts how Imam al-Sadiq publicly demonstrated that his son Isma'il had died, specifically to prevent people from later claiming that Isma'il was the hidden Mahdi.

The chapter recounts that Imam al-Sadiq publicly showed that his son Isma‘il had died, warning people not to claim later that Isma‘il was merely hidden as the Promised Mahdi. Mutahhari interprets the act as a deliberate effort to prevent a mistaken identification. The story illustrates why the death of a possible claimant could be made public evidence against a later claim of concealment.

chunks.title: The words of Di‘bil — A lamentation links past suffering with the awaited future
chunks.text:
Di'bil recited a lamentation before Imam al-Rida naming tragedies suffered by the Ahl al-Bayt. Imam al-Rida added a reference to a grave in Tus, identifying it as his own future grave, and the poem also connected the history of suffering with the eventual reappearance of an Imam.

Di‘bil recited a lamentation before Imam al-Rida that named tragedies suffered by the Ahl al-Bayt. The Imam added a reference to a grave in Tus, identifying his own future burial place. Mutahhari uses the poem and the Imam’s response to show how remembrance of past oppression and expectation of the Mahdi could coexist within one religious imagination; the lament was not only retrospective grief.

chunks.title: Mahdism in the Sunni World — The expectation crosses sectarian boundaries
chunks.text:
Mutahhari argues that Mahdism cannot be treated as exclusively Shi'ah by pointing to Sunni populations and historical figures who accepted or claimed Mahdist ideas.

Mutahhari argues that belief in the Mahdi is not exclusive to Shi‘ah communities. He points to Sunni reports and historical claimants, including the Mahdi of Sudan, as evidence that the expectation circulated more broadly. The presence of a belief across traditions does not make all interpretations identical or validate every claimant; it supports the narrower historical point that Mahdism had wide resonance.

chunks.title: Mahdism in the Sunni World — Why false claimants do not disprove the expectation
chunks.text:
The existence of false claimants is presented as another historical consequence of widespread belief in the promised Mahdi. Mutahhari distinguishes the existence of impostors from the truth of the underlying belief.

The chapter notes that false Mahdi claimants appeared in different places and traditions. Mutahhari treats their recurrence as a consequence of the expectation’s influence, while distinguishing impostors from the promised figure. Logically, the existence of false claimants neither proves nor disproves the underlying doctrine by itself; it shows why criteria and evidence are needed before accepting a specific person’s claim.

chunks.title: The words of Hafiz — Mahdist imagery without certainty about the poet’s sect
chunks.text:
Mutahhari notes Mahdist imagery in poems attributed to Hafiz, while explicitly saying he cannot establish whether Hafiz was Shi'ah or Sunni. The point is the presence of Mahdist expectation in Persian literary culture.

Mutahhari points to Mahdist imagery in poems attributed to Hafiz, but says he cannot establish whether Hafiz was Shi‘ah or Sunni. The example supports the claim that the idea had cultural and literary reach beyond a narrowly defined group. It also models a useful limit: a poem can show the presence of a theme without settling the poet’s precise doctrinal identity.

chunks.title: The essence of al-Mahdi’s uprising — Reform is not the enemy of reappearance
chunks.text:
Mutahhari addresses a dangerous interpretation: some people might think society must become maximally corrupt before the Imam can reappear, and therefore reform should be opposed. He rejects this reasoning.

Mutahhari rejects the idea that believers should oppose reform because society supposedly needs to become maximally corrupt before the Mahdi can appear. He argues that this would contradict religious duties such as prayer, moral education, enjoining good, and forbidding evil. A promise that justice will follow oppression is not permission to create or tolerate oppression.

chunks.title: The essence of al-Mahdi’s uprising — The abscess analogy and the limits of revolutionary thinking
chunks.text:
Mutahhari uses an abscess analogy to explain a revolutionary model in which accumulated corruption must reach a breaking point. He then contrasts this with the Islamic obligation to pursue reform rather than deliberately increase corruption.

Mutahhari contrasts a social model in which corruption must burst like an abscess with a model in which society ripens toward a more mature form. In his argument, reappearance is closer to the maturation of a fruit than to a demand that believers intensify corruption. The analogy is meant to challenge passivity and sabotage of reform, not to predict a simple linear path for history.

chunks.title: The essence of al-Mahdi’s uprising — Reappearance does not suspend religious duties
chunks.text:
Waiting for Imam al-Mahdi does not cancel prayer, fasting, zakat, Hajj, enjoining good, forbidding evil, or other personal and social obligations. Mutahhari presents this as a direct rejection of passive or destructive interpretations of waiting.

Mutahhari states that awaiting the Imam does not cancel prayer, fasting, zakat, Hajj, moral education, or social responsibility. He rejects the claim that believers should stop improving society in order to hasten the reappearance. The reasoning is direct: a doctrine about future justice cannot require people to violate the duties that the same religious tradition continues to impose.

chunks.title: The essence of al-Mahdi’s uprising — Awaiting requires action, not deliberate corruption
chunks.text:
The correct expectation of reappearance is compatible with fulfilling religious duties and training individuals and society. The believer does not create corruption in order to accelerate the promised transformation.

The chapter contrasts passive waiting with active preparation: worship, education, social reform, and enjoining good remain necessary. Mutahhari’s fruit analogy suggests that historical readiness depends on maturation and capability, not on intentionally making society worse. This is a central practical conclusion of the chapter and should not be diluted into a vague slogan that waiting means doing nothing.

chunks.title: Mahdism, a global philosophy — The historical survey gives way to a global vision
chunks.text:
Mutahhari closes the historical survey by moving from evidence for widespread Mahdist belief to the philosophical and practical meaning of awaiting the reappearance.

After surveying historical claims, Mutahhari says he wants to end with the wider meaning of Mahdism. He rejects reducing the doctrine to a local or ethnic hope that one community alone will become happy. The Qur’anic language he invokes concerns the earth and the righteous more broadly, so the promised future is framed as a global moral transformation.

chunks.title: Mahdism, a global philosophy — Justice after tyranny is not a command to produce tyranny
chunks.text:
The promise that justice will follow oppression does not mean believers should permit or create oppression. The promised future is not a justification for abandoning present moral responsibility.

Mutahhari returns to the risk that people may misuse predictions of future oppression as a reason to oppose present reform. His answer is that the promised end of tyranny does not make tyranny desirable or religiously required. A historical sequence described in prophecy is not an ethical instruction to help produce the evil that the prophecy says will eventually be overcome.

chunks.title: Mahdism, a global philosophy — The practical implication for believers today
chunks.text:
The chapter connects Mahdism to active religious responsibility: personal worship, social obligations and moral reform remain valid while awaiting the Imam.

The practical point is that belief in the Mahdi should shape current conduct: worship, social duty, education, and moral reform remain meaningful. Mutahhari’s argument rejects both despair about humanity and passivity disguised as religious expectation. The future vision is meant to orient present responsibility, not replace it.

chunks.title: Mahdism, a global philosophy — The evidence chain behind Mutahhari’s argument
chunks.text:
Mutahhari's historical chain is: Qur'anic promises → Prophetic reports → Imam 'Ali's statements → early Islamic Mahdist movements and claims → Sunni and Shi'ah historical evidence → practical meaning of awaiting reappearance.

The chapter’s historical case moves through several kinds of evidence: Qur’anic promises, Prophetic reports, statements attributed to Imam ‘Ali, early movements and claimants, and references across Sunni and Shi‘ah traditions. These kinds of evidence do different jobs. Scriptural themes establish a broad expectation; historical cases show the belief’s influence; neither should be treated as automatic proof of every individual claimant.

chunks.title: Mahdism, a global philosophy — Belief in the Mahdi versus political appropriation of the name
chunks.text:
A major exam distinction is between the doctrinal belief in a promised Mahdi and historical actors who appropriated the concept to legitimize political movements or particular claimants.

A recurring distinction is between the belief in a promised Mahdi and the use of that belief by political actors to legitimize themselves. Mukhtar, Nafs Zakiyyah’s supporters, and Abbasid rulers appear in different contexts and should not be treated as the same kind of claimant. Mutahhari’s point is that a doctrine can be historically influential while individual uses of it remain mistaken or manipulative.

chunks.title: Mahdism, a global philosophy — Separate historical evidence from interpretation
chunks.text:
Mutahhari repeatedly separates historical reports from his interpretation of their significance. Statements such as why a claimant acted, whether someone privately believed a claim, or how a movement should be judged may remain matters of interpretation.

Mutahhari repeatedly reports what a source says and then interprets why the report matters. A careful reader should preserve that boundary, especially when the chapter discusses motives, the authenticity of claims, or a poet’s religious affiliation. “A report exists” is not the same as “the report proves every conclusion drawn from it”; the reasoning between evidence and conclusion should be made explicit.

chunks.title: Mahdism, a global philosophy — Chapter 8’s conclusion: universal justice and the promised Imam
chunks.text:
The two-part chapter connects universal justice with Mahdism: justice is presented as the long-term direction of prophetic history, while the promised reappearance represents the culmination of that trajectory in a transformed human society.

The two parts of Chapter 8 connect universal justice with Mahdism. Part 1 asks whether humanity can become genuinely just; Part 2 traces the historical expectation of a promised leader and argues that awaiting him should sustain present responsibility. The chapter’s synthesis is both theological and ethical: hope for a just future is linked to how people act now.

chunks.title: Mahdism, a global philosophy — Awaiting as faith joined to responsibility
chunks.text:
The closing emphasis is that genuine awaiting is not passive pessimism. Mutahhari describes awaiting the reappearance as an expression of faith that coexists with worship, moral discipline, social responsibility and hope for humanity.

Mutahhari ends by presenting awaiting the reappearance as a high expression of faith, not an excuse to withdraw from the world. The believer is asked to prepare morally and socially while trusting in a future of justice. In this framing, hope and responsibility reinforce one another: the promise of a better future gives present reform meaning rather than making it unnecessary.

akhlaq.lesson: Do not turn hope for divine justice into political fantasy or passivity. Distinguish genuine evidence from claims, reject manipulation, and prepare for justice through responsible action now.
